title: Death as return
hookLine: death as a return, not an ending (2:156; 3:185)

cards: When a Muslim hears that someone has died, a neighbor's father, a celebrity, a friend's baby, the first words are very often the same. Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.

People say it in hospital corridors, in group chats, under their breath at the news, before they've even taken it in. And if you listen to the words, they don't mention death at all. They talk about going back home.

teach.h: WE ARE ALLAH'S, AND WE RETURN.
teach.b: Al-Baqarah, verse one hundred fifty-six, describes the patient as those who, when a misfortune strikes them, say, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning."
We belong to Allah, and to Him we return. Raji'un comes from r-j-', the root of going back to where you came from. Death, in this sentence, isn't a wall.

teach.h: EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.
teach.b: Al 'Imran adds the plain fact underneath: "Every soul will taste of death." No exceptions, and the verse says it without fear: the full reward comes on the Day of Resurrection.

Between death and that Day, surah twenty-three speaks of a barzakh, a barrier, a waiting. What it's like, the Qur'an doesn't describe in detail; the hadith say more, and scholars discuss them carefully.
A hadith in Sahih Muslim shows the words at work.
Umm Salamah heard the Prophet ﷺ teach that whoever is struck by loss and says, to Allah we belong and to Him we return, and asks Allah to reward them and replace it with better, will be given better.
When her husband Abu Salamah died, she said it, and thought, who could be better than Abu Salamah? Later the Prophet himself proposed to her. And graves aren't to be avoided.

Another hadith in Muslim's collection says: I had forbidden you to visit graves; now visit them. A second report there gives a reason: they remind you of death. A cemetery, in this vocabulary, isn't where things end.
It's a waiting room for a return.

how: Muslims say "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" on hearing of a death or any loss; they bury the dead quickly, pray the funeral prayer together, and visit graves, greeting the dead with peace.

o: mourning loudly for those who have died
a farewell for a soul gone for good
returning, going back to where we came from

games.q: death as return — tap the pairs.
p: every soul will taste of death
asked for better, and was given it

s: inna lillahi is only said when a Muslim dies
2:156 says it for any misfortune; it's said at any loss.
the Prophet at first forbade, then encouraged, visiting graves
now visit them; another report adds that graves remind you of death (Sahih Muslim).
the Qur'an describes the barzakh in detail
it names the barrier; the hadith say more, and scholars treat them carefully.

games.q: you're Umm Salamah. your husband has died. you've been taught to say: to Allah we belong, and ask for better. you think: who could be better? what do you do?
games.why: she said it anyway, and later the Prophet proposed to her (Sahih Muslim).

practice: Bring to mind someone who has died: their face, their hands, the sound of their voice, and don't push the grief away if it comes.
If you'd like, say the words softly, inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to Allah and to Him we return. If you pray, ask mercy for them, and stay with them a little longer.
